items.def: A deterministic AI-based system with a fixed unchanging model which does not change its behavior once it is deployed. E.g., a deployed DNN-based model whose weights and biases are fixed after development (self-driving car lane detection / traffic sign recognition).

An AI-based system that adjusts its behavior in response to changes in its operational environment. E.g., reinforcement learning adapting via a reward function; e-commerce recommendations based on evolving preferences.
The challenge of determining whether a test has passed or failed for a given set of test inputs and state.
The information provided by direct observation and measurement that is known to be real or true.

A systematic, often black-box form of fault attack that probes an AI-based system to identify harmful capabilities, particularly in its outputs — deliberately causing harmful or undesirable results (privacy violations, racist views, CBRN guidance), then using the findings to strengthen the system.
Ongoing, real-time defensive monitoring and filtering of inputs to an operational AI-based system to protect it against attacks; complements proactive, pre-deployment Red Teaming.

The challenge of testing a GenAI model whose inputs are highly diverse and hard to control: optional system prompts plus user prompts with enormous disparate data, API access, parameters (temperature, maximum tokens), and the context window — all affecting the output.

blocks.title: Locked vs adaptive, statistics, oracles, GenAI, test levels

items.text: Locked systems are far easier to test (largely deterministic, expected results don't change); an updated locked system is a NEW system needing fresh testing. Adaptive systems may change behavior during or because of testing; unpredictable behaviors can't be tested in advance — use automated suites re-run after significant changes plus threshold-based performance checks. Many GenAI/LLM systems sit between: locked at runtime, updated periodically. Even locked systems can show non-determinism (floating-point precision, hardware/parallel-GPU variation).

Why statistical testing — four reasons: Non-Determinism (single tests can't reflect overall correctness — suite must be large enough for statistical significance); Distributional Performance Evaluation (test a statistically significant sample from operational data distributions); Handling Uncertainty and Bias (quantify accuracy/fairness/robustness via confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, error analysis); Regulatory and Safety Context (demonstrate thresholds met with high confidence).

Test oracle problem causes: probabilistic/non-deterministic outputs (need thresholds/tolerance ranges); exploratory development with incomplete/missing specifications; task complexity beyond straightforward human verification; subjectivity of behavior (e.g., virtual assistant expectations vary); self-learning systems ('correct' evolves, initial expected results become invalid).

Oracle solutions: define output boundaries (acceptable ranges, distributions, limits, tolerances — e.g., car stops within max distance); define environmental boundaries (lighting, temperature, network latency for repeatability); expert consultation (opinions may differ or be fallible); specialized testing (A/B, back-to-back, metamorphic — compare behaviors/verify properties without explicit expected outputs); proxy oracles (secondary systems/models, e.g., image recognition checking generated images — beware reproducing similar biases/errors).

GenAI testing: black-box evaluation of correctness, coherence, creativity (clarity, originality, domain-rule adherence); manual review or a second GenAI system as judge (use carefully — may reproduce similar biases/errors); non-functional testing matters (CPU/GPU usage, memory, network bandwidth, response times for inference and training); benchmark suites give standardized, reproducible comparison across models.

Red teaming scope: especially critical for GenAI's vast attack space; covers security AND safety/privacy/fairness/bias/misinformation; security RT targets malicious inputs (indirect prompt injection, malicious content hidden in RAG documents) while safety RT finds harmful outputs under ordinary use (unsafe medical advice); regulatory expectation (EU AI Act); best run pre-deployment after initial quality assessments; core activity is interactive multi-turn prompting (e.g., 15-20 turns); coverage strategies: crowd-sourced prompts, automated LLM-generated attack prompts checked by another LLM, hybrid.

ML test levels: two ML-specific — input data testing (Ch 5: training + production data) and ML model testing (Ch 6: the models) — plus conventional levels: component (non-AI parts: UI, data pipeline, communication), component integration (data pipeline feeds model correctly; predictions exchanged/used correctly; API testing when AI-as-a-service), system (confirmation that ML functional performance survives embedding; e.g., after DNN compression;), system integration (external interfaces, representative conditions), acceptance (service suitability, ML functional performance criteria).

Risk-based ML testing: ML risks = project risks (development: algorithm, model development, framework — e.g., sub-optimal algorithm selection) + product risks (input data: biased/unrepresentative training data, pipeline defects; model: missed performance measures, overfitting, adversarial susceptibility). Risk areas map to the ML workflow: Development (Ch 7), Input data (Ch 5), Model (Ch 6); alternatively categorize by ISO/IEC 25059 quality characteristics.
Assemble a diverse team of testers to cover a wide range of perspectives and attack vectors.
Provide access to the AI-based system in a safe test environment.
Prompt the system to identify vulnerabilities, through open-ended exploration or using checklists.
Analyze the identified failures to understand threats.
Create datasets from these threats to support mitigations and system improvements.

Locked = fixed behavior post-deployment, mostly deterministic, expected results stable (but updates = new system + fresh testing; non-determinism possible from floating-point/GPU parallelism). Adaptive = evolves (reward function, new environments), may change during/because of testing — harder; unpredictable behaviors cannot be pre-tested.

items.confusion: Red teaming vs benchmarking vs blue teaming
items.text: RT = adaptive, dynamic, pre-deployment attacks (prompts updated in response to outputs), complements static benchmarking by testing extreme/unexpected conditions; Blue Teaming = ongoing real-time defensive monitoring/filtering of an operational system.

Security RT focuses on malicious inputs (indirect prompt injection, malicious content in RAG documents); safety RT targets harmful outputs under ordinary use without adversarial intent (e.g., unsafe medical advice).

items.confusion: Component integration vs system integration for MLS
items.text: Component integration = internal exchanges (data pipeline → model → UI, API testing for AI-as-a-service); system integration = interfaces and data exchanges with EXTERNAL systems/services under representative operational conditions.

items.confusion: Project risks vs product risks in ML
items.text: Project risks concern MLS development (sub-optimal algorithm selection, poor evaluation approach choice, framework security vulnerabilities); product risks concern the system itself (biased/unrepresentative training data, data-pipeline defects, overfitted model, adversarial susceptibility).
